evidence.title: A Randomized Controlled Trial and Pilot of Scout: an LLM-Based EHR Search and Synthesis Platform
evidence.outcome: Whether manual review of sampled outputs corrects the automated LLM-as-judge error flags
evidence.effect: Manual review of a subset found that most claims the automated judge flagged as errors were supported by the patient chart, so human validation was needed to estimate real error rates.
evidence.quote: Subsequent manual review of a subset of outputs revealed that most claims flagged by the automated judge as errors were in fact supported by the patient chart, demonstrating the importance of human validation.

evidence.title: Audited large language model triage for systematic review screening in national clinical guideline production: validation and prospective deployment
evidence.outcome: accuracy estimation via spot-checking outputs
evidence.effect: An audit of 600 randomly sampled AI-excluded records confirmed 0 final false negatives.
evidence.quote: Across 600 randomly sampled AI-excluded records from the migraine and dementia programmes, none was confirmed as a final false negative after post-unblinding adjudication; across the completed 680-record audit, all 38 final retained records had been AI flagged, whereas locked blinded human consensus missed seven.

evidence.title: Enhancing Aortic Aneurysm Surveillance: Transformer Natural Language Processing for Flagging and Measuring in Radiology Reports
evidence.outcome: Error counts of NLP output versus manual chart review as reference
evidence.effect: NLP had fewer errors than manual chart reviews: 12 vs. 22 (P = 0.084), 47 vs. 98 (P = 0.000021), and 31 vs. 53 (P = 0.015).
evidence.quote: Compared to manual chart reviews, the NLP system demonstrated superior accuracy and fewer errors: 12 vs. 22 (P = 0.084), 47 vs. 98 (P = 0.000021), and 31 vs. 53 (P = 0.015).

evidence.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Reducing Data Deluge From Cardiac Implantable Electronic Devices
evidence.outcome: AI classification accuracy versus blinded electrophysiologist adjudication on random ~15% sample of transmissions
evidence.effect: Against electrophysiologist gold standard, AI was 93.8% accurate with 99.1% sensitivity, 93% specificity, and F1 score of 81%.
evidence.quote: Considering electrophysiologist interpretation/adjudication as the gold standard, AI was 93.8% accurate with 99.1% sensitivity, 93% specificity, and an F1 score of 81%.

evidence.title: Large language models for automatable real-world performance monitoring of diagnostic decision support systems: a comparison to manual doctor panel review in a prospective clinical study
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM-automated vs clinician-review reference for estimating deployed DDSS accuracy
evidence.effect: GPT-5 eligibility accuracy 84.7% (κ = 0.57); exact diagnosis match 93.6% of 347 encounters; DDSS accuracy estimates indistinguishable at Top-1 and Top-3, one significant difference at Top-5.
evidence.quote: Diagnostic accuracy estimates based on manual versus GPT-5 mappings were statistically indistinguishable at Top-1 and Top-3 across the full analyzable sets, with one significant difference at Top-5.

evidence.title: Beyond Simulations: What 20,000 Real Conversations Reveal About Mental Health AI Safety
evidence.outcome: Clinician review audit of real deployed conversations for safety estimation
evidence.effect: Clinician review of 20,000 real conversations found zero suicide-risk cases lacking crisis resources and identified NSSI false negatives. The authors conclude ecological audits are useful for estimating safety.
evidence.quote: Findings support the utility of ecological audits for safety estimation.

evidence.title: Managing AI-Enabled Uncertainty in Clinical AI Deployment: Mixed-Methods Study of Governance, Workflow, and Organizational Learning in an ICU Decision Support Pilot
evidence.outcome: Whether live bedside benchmarking of predictions against actual outcomes served as a feedback mechanism
evidence.effect: Live benchmarking served as a feedback loop that supported model refinement, with mean absolute error falling from 5.95 to 4.12 days; 148 stays were benchmarked.
evidence.quote: Live benchmarking functioned as a feedback loop and supported exploratory model refinement, with CDSS mean absolute error decreasing from 5.95 to 4.12 days after the first model update.

evidence.title: Implementation of Human-in-the-Loop ChatGPT-based Patient Screening Across Multiple Diverse Clinical Trials
evidence.outcome: Criterion-level accuracy of deployed LLM outputs versus coordinator review
evidence.effect: Accuracy 0.94 (95% CI 0.92-0.96), sensitivity 0.98, specificity 0.81, PPV 0.95, NPV 0.93, F1 0.97 across 5,096 criteria reviewed by coordinators.
evidence.quote: Aggregated individual criterion-level performance: accuracy 0.94 (95% CI, 0.92–0.96), sensitivity 0.98 (0.97–0.99), specificity 0.81 (0.71–0.88), PPV 0.95 (0.92–0.97), NPV 0.93 (0.90–0.95), F1 0.97 (0.95–0.97).

evidence.title: A geometry and dose-volume based performance monitoring of artificial intelligence models in radiotherapy treatment planning for prostate cancer
evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Detection of clinically relevant AI errors by comparing AI output with clinician-corrected output
evidence.effect: Local Surface Dice 0.93±0.11 vs Standard 0.98±0.04 for anorectum (p=0.006); ADD 0.9±0.8 Gy anorectum D1cm3; combined metrics detected clinically relevant changes
evidence.quote: Combining dose-volume and geometrical metrics allowed detection of clinically relevant changes, applied to both auto-segmentation and auto-planning output and the Local Surface Dice was more sensitive to local changes compared to the Standard Surface Dice.

evidence.title: A retrospective audit of an artificial intelligence software for the detection of intracranial haemorrhage used by a teleradiology company in the United Kingdom
evidence.outcome: Agreement of deployed AI ICH detection outputs with radiologist review on sampled scans
evidence.effect: Overall agreement 93.5% (95% CI 92.1-94.8), PPA 85.7% (77.8-91.6), NPA 94.3% (92.8-95.5), Gwet's AC1 0.92; 16 false negatives, 9 were subarachnoid haemorrhages.
evidence.quote: Overall agreement, positive percent agreement, negative percent agreement, and Gwet's AC1 of AI with radiologists were found to be 93.5% (95% CI, 92.1-94.8), 85.7% (77.8-91.6), 94.3% (92.8-95.5) and 0.92 (0.90-0.94), respectively, in detecting ICH.

evidence.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
evidence.outcome: Periodic benchmark of every fifth DL plan against blinded manual plans
evidence.effect: Manual plans met all clinical goals in 16/16 vs mDLO 14/16; mDLO had lower spinal cord (30.3 vs 33.2 Gy) and parotid dose (15.8 vs 16.9 Gy).
evidence.quote: All clinical goals were met in manual plans for all patients ( n = 16) in the benchmark cohort, while mDLO plans reached all clinical goals in 14/16 patients (Supplementary Table S4).

evidence.title: Real-world use and evaluation of a generative AI chatbot for Parkinson's disease information: a prospective observational study

evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM-as-judge hallucination detection with human raters
evidence.effect: LLM judges reached up to 65.7% agreement on hallucination presence and 64.7% on subcategorization, described as reasonable alignment.
evidence.quote: Across automated hallucination detection, LLJs demonstrate reasonable alignment with human raters, achieving up to 65.7% agreement on hallucination presence and 64.7% agreement on hallucination subcategorization.

evidence.outcome: Agreement of automated AI-output quality checks with clinician ground-truth review
evidence.effect: The LLM QA tool showed moderate to strong agreement with expert judgments (ρ 0.733–0.794; quadratic weighted κ 0.730–0.798) across software.
evidence.quote: The LAQUA system demonstrated moderate to strong agreement with expert judgments across all evaluated software (ρ: 0.733–0.794; quadratic weighted κ: 0.730–0.798) and organs (ρ: 0.567–0.835; quadratic weighted κ: 0.639–0.804).

evidence.title: Using a Large Language Model for Postdeployment Monitoring of FDA-Approved Artificial Intelligence: Pulmonary Embolism Detection Use Case
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.outcome: Whether LLM-based report classification compared against deployed AI outputs detects discrepancies and drift
evidence.effect: Of 11,999 studies, 373 (3.1%) had discrepant classifications between CVPED and LLM; a 2.5% drop in LLM specificity led to a 1.7-fold increase in discrepancies, detected in 22 days.
evidence.quote: A PDM framework combining LLM-based free-text classification with a human-in-the-loop alerting system can continuously track an image-based AI's performance, alert for performance drift, and provide incremental clinical value.

evidence.title: Are Limited Electronic Medical Record Follow-Up Data Sufficiently Useful for Validating the Performance of Survival Prediction Models?
evidence.outcome: Whether EMR-only outcome data can estimate real-world model accuracy compared with higher-quality ground truth
evidence.effect: Discrimination estimates with EMR data matched the reference standard (C-index 0.67 vs 0.66), but calibration was misjudged: EMR-only data showed underprediction of survival while the reference showed reasonable calibration.
evidence.quote: When using reference standard data, the model was found to be reasonably calibrated, but with EMR data, the model was incorrectly found to systematically underpredict survival.

evidence.title: Importance of model governance in clinical AI models: case study on the relevance of data drift detection
evidence.outcome: monthly performance versus outcomes
evidence.effect: Monthly AUC monitoring found two below-limit months, March 2020 and March 2021; otherwise within ±3 SD.
evidence.quote: The AUC dipped slightly below our performance limit on two occasions: in March 2020 and March 2021.

evidence.title: Are Limited Electronic Medical Record Follow-Up Data Sufficiently Useful for Validating the Performance of Survival Prediction Models?
evidence.outcome: EMR-only performance monitoring validity
evidence.effect: EMR data validated discrimination, but not calibration; all-feature C-index/IBS were 0.67/0.16 with EMR only.
evidence.quote: EMR data were useful for validation of model discrimination, but not calibration.

commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-four studies, almost all from live deployments, found that comparing sampled AI outputs with clinician review, adjudication, or outcomes produced accuracy estimates and surfaced errors that automated checks missed. No study tested whether this practice reduces patient harm compared with not sampling, and most designs were descriptive, so certainty is low.

perspectives.view: The body includes one randomized trial, four prospective studies with a comparator, and nineteen descriptive, replay, or pre-post designs. Findings consistently show that sampled comparison yields usable accuracy estimates, and three studies report mixed results. Outcomes are accuracy and error detection rather than patient outcomes, which lowers directness. Certainty is rated low.

Clinician re-review found serious errors in 4 of 100 conversations that automated triage had rated good. Radiologist review of 1,315 head CTs found 16 missed haemorrhages, 9 of them subarachnoid. A stratified ED sample showed high within-stratum agreement but a design-weighted sensitivity of 0.40. This suggests that samples drawn only from flagged cases may overstate performance.

The choice of reference affects the estimate. LLM-extracted labels matched radiologist review closely (PPV 1, NPV 0.988), while LLM judges agreed with humans on hallucinations only up to 65.7%. Manual review showed most automated error flags were supported by the chart. EMR-only outcomes matched discrimination but misjudged calibration, and a change of reviewer coincided with a dip in scores.

The reported programs reviewed modest fractions of volume. One adjudicated about 15% of 690,673 transmissions, and another reviewed 1,160 of 593,365 mammograms over monthly cycles. An automated discrepancy check detected a 2.5% specificity drop within 22 days, and monthly AUC tracking flagged two months below limits. These findings suggest that partial automation may lower review staffing needs.

Only one of 24 studies reported enrolling limited English proficiency or older adult populations. That German study found errors missed by automated triage. No study reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients. None stratified accuracy estimates by these groups, so it remains unknown whether sampled review detects subgroup-specific failures.

Clinician review of 20,000 real conversations found no suicide-risk exchange that lacked crisis resources. The same review identified missed cases of non-suicidal self-injury. This suggests that human audit of real exchanges can find safety gaps that affect whether patients are directed to human help, though the study did not measure patient outcomes.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared sites that periodically sample outputs with sites that do not on patient harm, error correction time, or clinician trust. The literature does not establish how large or how frequent samples should be, and it does not show how to stratify samples so that low-prevalence misses are not underestimated. Evidence is also thin on how much reviewer turnover and inter-rater variability affect estimates, and on whether automated references such as LLM labels or EMR outcomes can stand in for human review when calibration matters.
commentary.underserved_note: One German study of deployed health conversations included limited English proficiency and older adult populations, and it found that sampled clinician review caught errors missed by automated triage. No study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so accuracy estimates from these programs may not reflect performance for those patients unless health systems stratify their samples.
